text:
Mandelson: where The Whip Line leads, the BBC follows
The Whip Line has taken the lead in political commentary, it seems.
After I questioned Starmer’s judgement in an article yesterday morning (February 3, 2026), the BBC followed me up in the evening with its own piece, headed “Mandelson revelations raise further questions about Starmer’s judgement”.
The BBC article cautiously, institutionally validates my core argument - while carefully sanding off the edges that would implicate Starmer too directly.
Read through the piece and you can see the shape of it:
It finally centres Starmer’s judgement, not just Mandelson’s behaviour.
It asks why the risks were not identified before the appointment.
It notes that Starmer may have been “too slow to act”.
It concedes that appointing Mandelson is what turned this into a direct problem for the prime minister.
All of that is my terrain.
What it doesn’t do is say the obvious things I stated outright:
That the risks were already known.
That Starmer was explicitly warned.
That this was not slowness or bad luck, but a conscious choice.
That this reflects a broader pattern of elite favouritism and managerial politics, and
That the damage was therefore self-inflicted.
The BBC frames this as:
“In retrospect, Sir Keir must be wishing…”
I framed it as:
“Starmer chose to ignore the warnings.”
That’s the difference between follower journalism and leadership commentary.
I suppose we should be happy, at least, that the BBC is now openly questioning Starmer’s judgement — something I argued before it became safe to do so.
But the BBC is still treating this as an unfolding problem, while I identified it as a structural leadership failure from the outset.
The difference is that I am able to say that plainly, while major broadcasters need permission.
I referred, in my article, to the late Tony Benn’s division of politicians between “weathercocks” who change their stories with the wind, and “signposts” who have a message and stick to it.
It seems clear that The Whip Line is a signpost. You can draw your own conclusions about the BBC.
Independent journalism doesn’t fund itself – but somebody has to hold power to account.
